The post Beyond the bursary: are we making a real difference with student financial support? appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Peter Gray, Chairman and CEO, JS Group. JS Group is a HEPI partner.

Despite the many millions of pounds that UK universities invest in financial support for their students through bursaries, scholarships, hardship funds and other means, there has traditionally been relatively little analysis of the difference this support makes, or how its impact could be strengthened.

The conversation often focuses on how much to invest, how much students are struggling financially or how much more support they need, rather than how effectively that support is delivered.

In the current financial climate, universities face the dual challenge of supporting students through significant financial pressures while ensuring that limited resources deliver maximum impact. Therefore, the more important question is: how do we ensure that the limited financial support available makes the greatest possible difference to the students receiving it?

We need to move beyond thinking about financial support simply in terms of expenditure and start considering how it can be designed around students’ real circumstances, enabling better experiences and outcomes.

What does the evidence tell us?

JS Group’s relationship with higher education stretches back to 1751, when John Smith opened a bookshop in Glasgow. Today we are a very different business; our work with universities gives us a valuable perspective on how financial support is delivered, accessed and used by students.

Our latest annual report, Beyond the Bursary: Rethinking Student Financial Support, draws on four years of activity across more than 45 higher education institutions, covering £352 million in financial support delivered to over 1.2 million beneficiaries, alongside feedback from 5,000 students. This provides a substantial evidence base to help universities better understand the factors that influence the effectiveness of their financial support.

In particular, we’ve identified the main considerations as timing and speed, along with control and capacity. This challenges us to think differently about what makes financial support genuinely effective.

Timing & speed: does financial support arrive when students need it most?

Students face considerable costs before arriving at university, from accommodation deposits and travel to essential equipment and learning resources. Yet much of our traditional thinking about student support begins after enrolment.

Our analysis highlights the importance of providing support earlier in the student journey, even before students have applied. The scale of this need is evident in the response to the Save the Student bursary (specifically designed to help cover essential costs when starting university), which attracted 2,685 applications for just six awards – almost 450 applications per bursary. From helping prospective students attend open days to providing digital access funding before term starts, early financial support can remove barriers at critical moments, influencing university choice and helping students arrive prepared.

Timing matters throughout the student journey – our data reveals clear peaks in demand for financial support, particularly as students stretch their finances between student finance payments and when unexpected financial difficulties arise. This highlights the importance of providing timely, flexible support that responds to students’ changing needs.

When students need urgent support, speed can be just as important as the amount provided. 90% of students said immediate access to funding was important, while 88% said receiving funding quickly reduced their stress or anxiety.

For a student struggling to pay rent, buy food or travel to lectures, waiting days or weeks for support can compound an already difficult situation. Universities must therefore consider not only whether support is available, but whether it can reach students at the moment it will make the greatest difference.

What difference does choice and control make?

Providing students with greater flexibility over when and how their funding is received and used can help them take greater responsibility for managing their finances. 89% of students said having control over when they accessed their funding helped them budget more effectively, while 86% reported a greater sense of independence.

But choice is also about providing the right form of support for different circumstances. An emergency payment to cover an unexpected bill, credit for essential learning resources or vouchers to help with everyday living costs can each serve a different purpose. The challenge for universities is to match the right support to the right student at the right time.

Financial support is about more than financial security; it creates capacity to participate

Perhaps the most significant findings concern the wider impact of financial support on students’ university experience. Among students receiving financial support, the proportion expressing concern about their finances fell from 70% before receiving support to 27% afterwards – a reduction of 43 percentage points.

But the benefits reported by students extended beyond reduced financial pressure. 77% said support helped them participate more in university life, 86% said it strengthened their sense of belonging, and 92% said it positively affected their student experience. Furthermore, 86% said the funding supported them in continuing their studies.

These are students’ reported experiences rather than proof of a direct causal relationship with institutional outcomes. Nevertheless, they highlight the important relationship between financial wellbeing, participation and the ability to make the most of higher education.

We often talk about student engagement, belonging and continuation as strategic priorities. Yet financial pressures can prevent students from participating in the very activities and opportunities that help them feel part of their university community.

Effective financial support can create the capacity for students not simply to remain in higher education, but to engage with it more fully. And the benefits may extend beyond graduation, through greater financial confidence, independence and resilience.

From delivering support to designing it for impact

What does all this mean for universities? In a sector facing significant financial constraints, the answer is not necessarily to spend more, but to ensure that existing investment delivers the greatest possible benefit.

Our analysis shows that the method, timing and purpose of financial support all matter. Understanding how funding is used, when students need it and the difference it makes should inform future decisions about its design.

Different circumstances call for different approaches. Cash, credit for books and essential resources, vouchers for groceries or fuel and other forms of support can each play a role, depending on what students need to achieve.

This requires universities to ask three fundamental questions:

When will support make the greatest difference?

How should it be delivered to reflect students’ circumstances?

For whom can it remove the greatest barriers to participation and success?

After 275 years working alongside universities, we recognise that students’ needs and institutional challenges will continue to evolve. Our approach to financial support must evolve too.

The opportunity is to move beyond measuring financial support by the amount distributed and towards understanding the outcomes it helps make possible.

Effective financial support is not simply a question of how much is provided. It is a question of how well that support is designed around students’ real circumstances.

That is what it means to move beyond the bursary.

REGISTER for ‘Invest now or pay later? The future of professional services in higher education’ webinar, Thursday 12 November, 12pm – 1pm

HEPI is hosting a webinar on Thursday 12 November from 12pm to 1pm to explore the findings of The invisible majority (HEPI Report 205), a study of the professional and support staff who make up 56 per cent of the UK higher education workforce and 48 per cent of its pay bill.

These staff run student services, maintain buildings, manage research grants and operate digital systems. Yet most institutions respond to financial pressure through restructuring, hiring freezes and outsourcing, cutting the very capability they need to recover.

Drawing on surveys of 450 respondents, the report finds that three-quarters face sustained high work intensity and two-thirds say change has affected them negatively, rising to 79 per cent of those earning below £40,000. Jobs have expanded without redesign, and change is too often done to staff rather than with them.

This webinar will unpack the report’s evidence and recommendations, from reforming job evaluation to fixing the sector’s workforce data and discuss how universities can protect the capability they depend on while budgets are tight. It will offer clear evidence and practical insight into the choice between investing now and paying later.

Speakers include:

Professor Sir Steve West CBE, Vice-Chancellor, President and Chief Executive, University of the West of England (UWE), Bristol

Margaret Ayers, Chief People Officer, University of the Arts London, and Chair, Universities Human Resources (UHR)

Cheryl Watson, VP Education, UK, TechnologyOne

Amanda Owen-Meehan, Consulting Director, AHEP Consulting

Nick Hillman OBE (Chair), Chief Executive, HEPI

REGISTER for ‘Using AI to make students smarter’ webinar, Tuesday 17 November, 12pm – 1pm

Join HEPI and Studiosity for a webinar on Tuesday 17 November on ‘Using AI to make students smarter‘.

The Student Generative AI Survey 2026 (HEPI Report 199) found that 94% of students use generative AI to help with assessed work and that 65% think that assessment has changed significantly in response to AI, with some expressing anxiety about the possibility of false accusations of misconduct. At the same time, while 68% of students believe AI skills are essential in today’s world, only 48% feel supported by their teaching staff to develop these skills.

Universities around the world are grappling with how best to respond to the rapid development of AI: supporting students to use AI ethically, critically and transparently, while at the same time, mitigating the risks of inappropriate use and trying to address inequalities in access to the latest tech. Recent HEPI research, What UK university AI policies actually do: A study of 96 institutions (HEPI Policy Note 71), by Professor Sam Illingworth, found that the majority of publicly-available university AI policies reflect a model of conditional trust, in which students are trusted only if they declare their use of AI, retain evidence and submit their work to verification. This complements a previous article by Professor Rose Luckin, published in AI and the Future of Universities (HEPI Report 193), which argues that universities should shift from concerns about cheating to a broader reconsideration of how to increase students’ human intelligence in order that they might thrive in a world of increasingly sophisticated tools.

How should higher education institutions and their partners respond to AI in ways that prioritise learning over detection, building trust at scale, and developing students’ skills, while addressing the risks of misuse?

Speakers include:

Professor Sam Illingworth, Professor of Critical AI Literacy, Edinburgh Napier University

Professor Kelly Coate, Provost, Richmond American University London

Graeme Kirk, Partnership Development Lead, Studiosity

Nick Hillman OBE, Chief Executive, HEPI (Chair)

Hosted with support from Studiosity.

https://us06web.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_o580rY7TR2qehkye9sEWgQ

REGISTER for ‘Big is beautiful? What should the future shape and size of the higher education sector look like?’ webinar, Wednesday 25 November, 1pm – 2pm

On Wednesday 25 November, join HEPI and Ellucian for a lunchtime webinar featuring guest speakers including Dr Dan Greenstein, former Chancellor of the Pennsylvania State System of Higher Education, and author of HEPI’s recent report Risk and Resilience: What UK higher education can learn from the United States.

As higher education institutions grapple with unprecedented challenges and come under heightened pressure to collaborate, how should the sector organise itself? The landscape is changing fast, with mergers, takeovers and possible closures all in the news. What should the future size and shape of UK institutions and the higher education sector as a whole look like? What can we learn from the United States, where hundreds of higher education institutions and thousands of campuses are thought to have closed in recent years due to demographic change and other factors?

In a recent HEPI Policy Note, Dr Dan Greenstein argued that institutional leaders should prioritise revenue growth over all else, but others have argued such growth brings its own problems over time. So should individual institutions primarily search for collaboration and growth, and if so, how? Or should institutions continue to emphasise what makes them special and distinct, even if this keeps them small? Which path offers greater protection from increased vulnerability and is more likely to protect diverse provision?

title: Scottish colleges need £2.5bn  investment boost by 2037, report warns
summary: A new report has laid bare the financial challenges facing Scotland's college sector.
full_text:
Colleges in Scotland will need £2.5bn to meet required investment in their infrastructure over the next decade, according to a new report.

The Scottish Funding Council (SFC) estimated £1.3bn was needed to maintain the college estate to a good standard, while an additional £1.2bn would be required to fund improvements.

The College Infrastructure Investment Plan (College IIP) said the "condition, configuration and expense" of some further and higher education buildings meant they were "no longer fit for purpose".

Colleges Scotland chief executive, Gavin Donoghue, said the report laid bare the "scale of the challenge" facing the sector.

The SFC is the body which allocates public funding to higher education.

This report covers all of Scotland's 24 colleges - which are spread across 99 campuses and 270 buildings - and spans a 10-year period between 2027/28 and 2036/37.

It said about £200m of the required funding would need to be used to tackle a maintenance backlog.

But the SFC warned only dealing with the most urgent investment needs would result in further deterioration of college infrastructure.

Donoghue said investment needed in 2027/28 alone was estimated at £262m.

He said a flat cash settlement from the Scottish government's budget on 3 December would "barely allow some institutions to address their most urgent issues".

Donoghue added: "Colleges need modern, sustainable and digitally enabled learning environments if they are to continue supporting learners, employers and Scotland's ambitions for productivity, net zero and inclusive growth.

"Investing in colleges would be a key part of ensuring colleges have a firm future as civic anchors as the public sector reforms and changes in the coming years."

Scottish colleges are publicly funded, have no borrowing options and are highly dependent on grants from the SFC.

That is in contrast to universities, which benefit from research income, international student fees and private donations.

A previous SFC report warned "insolvency remains an imminent risk" at some of the country's colleges.

Only three are currently forecast to break even.

The combination of an extensive backlog of maintenance, Raac issues and problems with cladding are central to the issues with infrastructure.

However, many buildings also require to be modernised and that pressure combines to create the £2.5bn figure in the report.

Paul Devoy, interim chief executive of the SFC, said: "This report underlines the need for change if we are to realise our ambitions within the funding available.

"It will now provide the foundation for our work with colleges to consider realistic, affordable and sustainable options for future reform that will deliver high-quality learning environments for future generations."

Tertiary Education Minister Alyn Smith said the Scottish government was aware a "significant transformation" was required across the college sector to guarantee its long-term future.

He said the government was working with Colleges Scotland and the SFC to create the "college sector of the future" which would aim to shape colleges for the next generation.

Smith added: "Scotland's colleges play a vital role in our economy and wider society, and this report is a useful piece of work on the extent to which their collective estate will need significantly more funding over the next ten years unless things change.

"We are well aware that significant transformation is required across the sector to guarantee its long-term future, which is why we provided a 10% uplift in core college funding to £764m in this year's budget."

The post OPINION: Want K-12 students engaged with civics? Teach them the math behind democracy, so they know why they need to vote appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
Democracy runs on mathematics. Tallying votes, allocating legislative seats and drawing district maps all depend on mathematical choices that can produce dramatically different outcomes.

Math provides a common language that shifts attention away from partisan ideology and toward cooperation, neutrality and shared facts. It sheds light on democracy’s structural problems and provides a way to create systems that are fairer and more resilient.

At a moment when educators are rethinking how to prepare students for an increasingly complex world, the mathematics of democracy offers a rare opportunity to teach intellectually rigorous, consequential topics that can build awareness and capacity.

Decisions about which topics to prioritize teaching are often framed as zero-sum. If we teach art, then we cannot also teach personal finance. If we prioritize math, science and English language arts, then social studies and civics need to take the back seat.

We believe it doesn’t have to be that way. Having to choose between teaching math and civics is a false dichotomy. Educators can and should teach concepts at the intersection of math and civics, such as voting methods, gerrymandering, the Electoral College, proportional representation and political data analysis.

Related: A lot goes on in classrooms from kindergarten to high school. Keep up with our free weekly newsletter on K-12 education.

The only way to fully understand the key mechanisms of democracy is through learning their conceptual mathematical foundations. Further, civics concepts can make math relevant and engaging for students to learn.

For example, discussing voter turnout — analyzing voter characteristics such as age, family income and race/ethnicity — can help develop an understanding of statistics and data visualization. It can also encourage students to think about why turnout is uneven among different groups.

Comparing election outcomes across various tallying methods provides a better understanding of functions and counting techniques.

And fractions become more concrete and relevant when students use them to proportionally allocate government representatives among geographic areas.

Although schools teach mathematics as a core subject and civics has recently gained renewed attention, the two remain largely compartmentalized. We are working to build widespread support for introducing and scaling math-civics concepts in K-12 schools. Our first step was to learn about current practices and the barriers to and pathways for bringing these topics to more classrooms, so our University of Southern California and Wellesley College research team interviewed 123 educators and curriculum providers across six states: California, Florida, Illinois, Massachusetts, New York and Texas.

Participants included teachers, school officials, district and state education leaders and math and civics curriculum providers across elementary, middle and high school contexts.

Educators in all these groups expressed enthusiasm for math-civics topics because they connect classroom learning to students’ real questions, such as “When am I going to use this in real life?”

Many also viewed math-civics literacy as a way to reduce polarization, strengthen democracy and empower future voters and leaders.

The educators who had already integrated math-civics concepts into their instruction said students learned to identify flaws in democratic institutions and evaluate democratic reforms, thus preparing these future voters to demand greater transparency and accountability from public officials.

Proponents of teaching math-civics concepts in math classes said they saw it as a compelling way to teach real-world applications. Those supporting math-civics concepts in civics/social studies classes noted that related topics already appear in their courses, and civics standards may allow more flexibility for interdisciplinary instruction.

Interviewees also saw opportunities across grade levels: Elementary grades lend themselves to interdisciplinary teaching because a single teacher typically teaches multiple subjects. District and state social studies curriculum requirements often feature middle school civics courses, and math-civics concepts align well with middle school math standards. High schools could incorporate math-civics units in AP Statistics, government, economics or electives, though elective-only models would miss many of the students who would benefit the most.

Related: STUDENT VOICE: My generation knows less about civics than my parents’ generation did, yet we need it more than ever

Despite clear enthusiasm, respondents said there is very little teaching on the mathematical foundations of democracy. Where it exists, math-civics instruction is usually tied to election-cycle activities or depends on individual teachers’ intitiative rather than a systemic approach.

The result is minimal instruction on these topics at a time when debates over ranked-choice voting, districting and the merits of the Electoral College are increasingly occupying the public square.

This omission leaves citizens less able to evaluate democratic systems as fair or representative and more vulnerable to misinformation and disenfranchisement.

That is why, drawing on our research, we are defining what we consider to be desired learning outcomes and aligning them to existing state standards. We will contact state departments of education and ask that they include math-civics concepts in student learning standards. We are also reaching out to a recently announced panel that is developing a new student civics learning framework to suggest including math-civics concepts. As another approach, we will partner with a core math curriculum provider and districts to pilot pedagogical supports for teachers.

Without a mathematical component, education for citizenship leaves students only partially prepared for democratic participation. Civic quantitative literacy is therefore not a luxury but a prerequisite for a healthy democracy.

Anna Saavedra serves as the director of the Center for Civic Society within the University of Southern California Schaeffer Institute for Public Policy and Government Service.

Ismar Volić is a Wellesley College professor of mathematics and co-founder and director of the Institute for Mathematics and Democracy.

Contact the opinion editor at opinion@hechingerreport.org.

title: Tech companies enlist colleges to help them train data center workers
summary:

The post Tech companies enlist colleges to help them train data center workers appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
The artificial intelligence race has been a boon for construction workers, employing many thousands nationwide as sprawling data centers rise from the dirt.

Eventually, the construction sounds will give way to a steady whir or whine emitted from giant, nondescript buildings filled with racks, servers, cables and cooling systems. Then what?

That’s the question vexing economists and county planners alike. The outlook for whether data centers will boost regional economies after construction subsides remains fuzzy. A site that generated thousands of construction jobs for several months or a few years may only employ several hundred or fewer employees long term.

But at least some workers will be needed to keep the buildings humming. Increasingly, the very corporations building data centers are playing a key role in training the operational workforce. Microsoft, Amazon, Google and Oracle are among the companies partnering with local higher education institutions to mint data center technicians and skilled trades workers, with the promise of in-demand jobs.

“It’s those mid-level jobs — the server technicians, the hardware technicians, those that have to maintain the infrastructure,” said Scott Adams, a professor of economics at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee. “There are hundreds of those jobs that are necessary, and those jobs need training because, in a sense, nobody has kind of done this explicit job before.”

The training programs exist in practically all corners of the United States. Just to name a few: Columbus State Community College in Ohio offers a data center technician program in partnership with Amazon Web Services. New Mexico State University and the University of New Mexico work with Oracle Academy. Gateway Technical College in Wisconsin houses a Microsoft Datacenter Academy.

Despite the potential benefits of these workforce training programs, they’re publicized only lightly through a few press releases or information posted online. Google, Oracle and Microsoft either didn’t respond to or declined interview requests from The Hechinger Report. These companies have encountered increasing resistance from local communities about the construction of data centers.

But 30-year-old Louis Maxcy is among a growing number of data center technicians whose career was jumpstarted by a scholarship-funded training program. He started courses for that program in September 2025 at Oregon’s Blue Mountain Community College, which partners with Amazon Web Services. The company hired him in the spring as he continued his training, giving him the cooperative work experience he needed to complete the program. In June, he graduated with a certificate and a job.

Now, he drives less than 10 minutes to an AWS data center in his hometown of Umatilla, in northeastern Oregon. The area’s economy is largely agricultural, and the largest employer is a state prison.

“There’s always been a stigma in this area that if you want to be successful, you need to leave,” Maxcy says.

He adds that his career path is proof that’s not the case anymore.

Related: Interested in innovations in higher education? Subscribe to our free biweekly higher education newsletter.

The data center building frenzy has dominated global headlines, thanks to massive capital investments and concerns ranging from power and water usage to noise pollution. Data Center Map, which has been compiling market research since 2007, shows more than 4,700 locations across the U.S., with large clusters in Virginia, Texas, Ohio, California, Georgia and Illinois.

The U.S. Census Bureau estimates that employment in data centers increased more than 60 percent from 2016 to 2023. But the number of sustained operational jobs within data centers varies.

Even so, training programs are attempting to address a skills gap as data centers rapidly multiply and companies need qualified workers to run them.

Amazon Web Services, a cloud computing pioneer dating back to 2006, needs technicians who take care of data centers’ computer hardware as well as building operations and machinery, says Nicholas Lee-Romagnolo, the company’s principal for workforce and economic development. Those positions require varying levels of technical skill in a constantly evolving environment.

“Those servers change all the time. The fiber changes all the time,” Lee-Romagnolo said. “Everything inside the data center is constantly being upgraded, especially in Amazon Web Services’ data centers. So we have to make sure that curriculum isn’t 3 years old — that it’s constantly being updated to serve the present need.”

That’s where partnerships with colleges come in.

Related: As college graduates fret over finding jobs, a record shortage of workers is predicted

Last fall, Gateway Technical College in Racine, Wisconsin, launched a Microsoft Datacenter Academy. It’s one of several dozen around the world. Microsoft declined an interview request, but the technology company’s website describes the academy as a “community skilling program that collaborates with local education partners to create pathways into the datacenter industry.”

The timing and location aren’t random. In June, Microsoft opened its first data center in the Village of Mount Pleasant, which sits between Milwaukee and Chicago in Racine County. Construction of a second, adjacent facility is underway.

During two semesters at Gateway, students can complete four courses — IT Tech Skills, Hardware/Software Support, Server Technologies and Data Center Technician — to receive a Microsoft Data Center Certificate.

If those courses sound more skills-based than conceptual, that’s the whole point. Step into a classroom and you’ll find students peering into the organs of a standalone computer or server, said Mark Kappes, dean of Gateway’s Business and Workforce Solutions, which oversees partnerships with employers, and its School of Manufacturing, Engineering and Information Technology.

He said the “hands-on” courses prepare students to step right into roles as data center technicians, IT support specialists, cloud infrastructure associates or facilities operation technicians. Large hyperscalers and smaller companies with data storage needs employ technicians to monitor and replace hardware, troubleshoot problems and ensure overall facility safety.

By the end of May, 14 students had earned the Microsoft Data Center Certificate, and another 206 were enrolled in the program, Kappes said. Recent high school graduates and adults seeking a career pivot have been especially interested thanks to scholarships Microsoft funds, for the program and for some IT students, which cover the $2,277 tuition and approximately $760 for books.

Another part of the allure? A fast track to a job in an emerging sector. Students who complete the certificate can directly enter the workforce or continue pursuing a degree. Some do both.

“It has Microsoft’s name on it, and Microsoft is sponsoring scholarships for it, but it’s not necessarily to drive people or students or graduates to Microsoft,” said Kappes. “It’s for the general community’s well-being.”

Indeed, pushback about data centers often revolves around the perceived drawbacks versus the potential community benefits of greenlighting such projects. A report from the Brookings Institution, a think tank, released earlier this year urged local governments to negotiate stronger regional benefits when they strike deals with tech companies, such as investments in job training for local residents that could foster an evolving tech employment ecosystem.

“We’ve seen [workforce training] just pop up organically in the wild,” said Mark Muro, who co-authored the report. “The next step is for this to become a kind of standard part of negotiations.”

Steven Zylstra, president and CEO of the Arizona Technology Council, a networking and trade association, sees some parallels with the semiconductor industry, which has teamed up with community colleges to bolster its workforce pipeline. Maricopa Community Colleges in Arizona, for instance, have partnerships with Intel for training manufacturing facility technicians and Microsoft for preparing data center technicians.

“The demand is growing, and obviously companies know exactly what they need,” he said. “When they develop these internal programs, they get what they’re expecting.”

Related: Colleges struggle to make manufacturing jobs hot again

Will students get what they are expecting?

Data center training programs provide an entry point to modern jobs with livable wages and benefits, especially for people who lack interest in a four-year degree or cannot afford it.

The average wage for data center technicians is about $32 an hour, based on 7,700 Indeed job postings over the last three years, which comes out to roughly $66,000 a year. Managers or specialized roles can command six-figure salaries, though more education may be necessary.

Still, experts say students should ask questions about the portability of the skills they’re learning and whether their knowledge could, ironically, become obsolete, thanks to the quick pace of AI innovation.

Chad Knights, chief academic officer and vice president of academic affairs at Northern Virginia Community College, thinks students at his institution will be well positioned to adapt to changes. He said NOVA, which partners with AWS and other companies to train aspiring data center workers, has a curriculum that is intentionally well-rounded.

“It’s a very AI-resilient role,” he said, pointing to the manual processing, troubleshooting and physical infrastructure management aspects of the job. “But even if it does become subject to some level of automation, those individuals have their hand in no less than four different trades: plumbing, HVAC, electrical and fiber.”

Adams, the economics professor at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, agreed that the AI economy appears to be turning away from an occupation-based model, where workers solely identify by specific titles, and moving instead toward one that prizes a suite of skills. An employee may label himself as a welder who specializes in heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems.

“We’re kind of at the beginning of the railroad,” Adams said. “We’re just laying some tracks … and I think nobody could envision 150 years ago how that would change the economy and the new jobs that would be created.”

Maxcy, the data center technician in Oregon, says his new job provides constant learning opportunities. Every day brings new problems to solve or efficiencies to discover while keeping the sprawling data center’s servers operating. He monitors, troubleshoots and repairs servers — often debriefing with colleagues on other teams afterward.

“We can kind of compare notes and talk about how we can grow as technicians from what the other person is learning,” he said.

Maxcy originally wanted to study computer science. He earned two associate degrees before switching to the data center technician training program, which he thought offered a more viable career pathway.

He now considers his work akin to a modern-day trade.

“In a lot of ways, I feel like I’ve made it,” said Maxcy, who envisions a long career working for Amazon Web Services. “I feel like I’m comfortable, and I have a good, sustainable income to thrive in this area.”

title: 5 Challenges to Student Well-Being in the Digital Age
summary:
5 Challenges to Student Well-Being in the Digital Age
Joshua.Bay Tue, 11/03/2026 - 03:00 AM

From social media use to digital gambling, emerging concerns about student well-being are prompting colleges to rethink their approaches to technology.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Technology has increasingly become central to the college experience, influencing how students learn, communicate, build relationships and navigate challenges both in and outside the classroom.

But as digital platforms and artificial intelligence become more embedded in students’ daily lives, questions are emerging about how those technologies affect their mental health and overall well-being.

Recent research and reporting highlight the complicated relationship between technology use and student well-being, including the links between social media and loneliness, the growing use of AI for emotional support, and concerns about excessive internet use and digital gambling. At the same time, some institutions are exploring ways to encourage students to disconnect from their devices and engage more intentionally with their campus communities.

Here are five takeaways from recent Inside Higher Ed Student Success coverage on the challenges and opportunities related to supporting student well-being in the digital age.

Social media use is linked to loneliness.

More than half of college students nationwide may experience loneliness, according to new research from the University of Cincinnati, which also found that those who spend the most time on social media are particularly likely to feel isolated.

The study, based on survey data from nearly 65,000 students ages 18 to 24 across more than 120 colleges nationwide, found that spending just 16 hours a week—a little more than two hours a day—on social media was linked with higher rates of loneliness.

Loneliness was measured by asking students how often they felt left out, lacked companionship or felt isolated. Students were also asked how many hours they spent on social media in a typical week. About 13 percent of students were classified as excessive social media users, defined as spending at least 16 hours a week online.

Students who used social media for 16 to 20 hours a week were 19 percent more likely to report feeling lonely than those who didn’t use it at all. The difference grew to 23 percent among those who spent 21 to 25 hours a week online and 34 percent among those who spent 26 to 30 hours. The heaviest users—those spending at least 30 hours a week on social media—were 38 percent more likely to report feeling lonely.

Madelyn Hill, an assistant professor at Ohio University who led the study while completing her doctoral work in the University of Cincinnati, said colleges should take a more proactive approach to educating students about the potential effects of excessive social media use, including encouraging them to set time limits and prioritize in-person connections. “Increasing educational campaigns and messaging around that is important,” she said.

Excessive internet use raises concerns, especially for young men.

Student success professionals are particularly worried about loneliness, social isolation and belonging among young men, who are less likely to seek mental health support than women. But the challenges facing them extend beyond mental health, intersecting with how they spend their time online and their relationships with others.

The two-day Symposium on Young American Men, held in Washington, D.C., in September, brought together lawmakers, researchers, journalists and organizational leaders to examine challenges facing young men and potential policy solutions. Discussions focused on issues ranging from declining college enrollment and mental health to technology use and economic opportunity, highlighting how these challenges intersect and shape young men’s futures.

For higher education leaders, those overlapping pressures raise questions about what colleges can do to better support young men’s well-being and success. Survey research released during the symposium found that more than half of men between the ages of 18 and 30 spend over five hours online each day.

Businessman and political commentator Andrew Yang described how isolation and excessive internet use can compound the challenges facing young men.

“Too many of our young men are not getting out there. They’re staying at home. They’re in their parents’ basements. They’re going down internet rabbit holes. They’re becoming radicalized,” Yang said. “I want people to reflect on what that means for that individual, but also their family and their community. This is one of the foremost challenges of our time.”

AI is becoming a source of emotional support.

As institutions nationwide struggle to meet growing mental health needs, more students are turning to AI for comfort, connection and advice. Now, colleges and universities face a once-unthinkable question: What happens when students begin opening up to AI chatbots instead of people?

Alison Lee, chief research and development officer of The Rithm Project—a nonprofit focused on fostering meaningful human connection in the age of AI—joined Inside Higher Ed’s Voices of Student Success podcast to discuss why young people are increasingly turning to AI for emotional support and what the shift could mean for higher education.

While conversations about AI and student mental health often swing between hype and fear, Lee said the reality of how young people are using the technology is more nuanced, and higher education leaders are still working to understand its implications.

Last fall, the nonprofit surveyed nearly 2,400 people ages 13 to 24, including more than 500 young adults ages 18 to 24, about how their AI use intersects with their social lives, emotional well-being and relationships.

“What was really powerful was when we started to drill into their AI use, what we found was that about one in three young people were talking to AI either for emotional or relational support or were talking to an AI character,” Lee said. “While one in three is not a majority, it’s not an insignificant number.”

Colleges may be overlooking digital gambling.

Digital wagering—from online sportsbooks like FanDuel and DraftKings to prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket, where users trade on much more than sports—has exploded in recent years. So has their marketing on social media and other platforms, including sports broadcasts.

But data on student digital wagering and how institutions are responding to its rise has been limited. New findings from two parallel surveys by Inside Higher Ed, one of undergraduates and another of student success administrators, offer insight into the issue. The student findings come from Inside Higher Ed’s annual Student Voice survey with Generation Lab of 5,034 undergraduates from 310 mostly public two- and four-year institutions.

Most institutions aren’t tracking digital wagering on their campuses, but 15 percent of student respondents say they’ve participated in online sports betting, prediction-market trading or other digital wagering since enrolling in college. Among men, that figure rises to 25 percent, while 12 percent of undergraduates ages 25 and older report having wagered online.

While just 11 percent of student success administrators surveyed say their institution considers digital wagering an escalating mental health or financial safety crisis, much larger shares of students believe the issue deserves more attention. Nearly half of male undergraduates and a third of women at least somewhat agree that digital wagering is a problem their institution is not adequately addressing.

“Digital wagering and gambling should be part of the standard prevention conversation on campus,” said Jhenai W. Chandler, vice president for research and policy at NASPA–Student Affairs Administrators in Higher Education. “It also belongs in our discussions about mental health, financial aid and financial wellness, because the consequences show up in all those places.”

Disconnecting can foster connection.

As colleges increasingly incorporate technology and artificial intelligence into the student experience, Cornell University is asking its campus community to consider a different question: When might students be better off without it?

In September, students, faculty and staff participated in Cornell Unplugged, a new weeklong initiative encouraging the campus community to decrease technology use and increase face-to-face interaction.

The initiative encourages participants to put down their devices during meals, attend in-person events and spend more time engaging with classmates and nature. Faculty members are also encouraged to consider tech-free or tech-light exercises in their classrooms.

Cornell Unplugged is designed to get participants thinking about their relationship with technology across three areas: how excessive use can contribute to social isolation and disconnection, whether unplugging can encourage more thoughtful and human-centered approaches to teaching and learning, and the environmental costs associated with computing and AI.

“There’s never going to be a one-size-fits-all solution, and there are certainly many and important and essential uses of technology in the learning environment,” said Steven Jackson, chair of the Cornell Sustainable Computing Working Group and vice provost for academic innovation. “The Cornell Unplugged initiative is really about deepening that conversation about where the uses are helpful and where the uses are counterproductive or damaging to student learning.”

title: The Fight for the Future of Democratic Foreign Policy
full_text:
The midterm elections mark the beginning of the Democratic Party’s 2028 presidential campaign. After two years of debate over the lessons of Kamala Harris’s defeat in the 2024 election, it promises to be one of the most open contests about the future of Democratic policies, including foreign policy, in generations. It also promises to be one of the most consequential. The strategic environment in 2029 is on track to be the most difficult and unforgiving since the height of the Cold War.

Democrats must therefore lay out their ideas early and see how they fare both with voters and against the trajectory of world events. The party is generally split into two camps: centrists who, when it comes to foreign policy, are focused on strategic competition, restoring the United States’ national power, and deepening alliances; and progressives, who propose a more affirmative agenda emphasizing shared challenges and global cooperation. In many ways, this divide has become familiar. But as the second Trump administration continues its project of overturning the post–World War II global order, the debates within each camp are at least as important as the disagreements between them.

If the party’s major foreign policy disagreements—on the future of the international order, on Israel, on artificial intelligence, on China, and on the global economy—are not litigated by prospective candidates, former officials, and prominent thinkers now, and voters are not given the chance to make an informed choice between coherent options, the first year of a Democratic administration could be consumed by indecision and infighting. Democrats must therefore understand where they stand on each of those questions, where centrists and progressives converge, and where the sharpest divisions now lie.

AFTER BIDEN

The three Democratic presidents since the end of the Cold War have all made some version of a U.S.-led international order a cornerstone of their foreign policy. But although former President Joe Biden’s rhetoric, with its emblematic “America Is Back” catchphrase, gestured at restoring that order after Trump, Biden did not govern like a restorationist. For the Biden administration, in which I served, the intensifying strategic competition with China and Russia and the onset of shared challenges such as the pandemic marked an external unraveling of the old era that necessitated major changes in U.S. strategy. Biden shifted foreign economic policy away from free trade and globalization toward industrial policy, resilience, and technological leadership, and he pushed back more assertively against Beijing and Moscow than did his Democratic predecessors.

As they reflect on the Biden administration, centrists are actively debating whether a future Democratic administration can restore and reform the U.S.-led international order or whether the United States must adapt to a prolonged period of geopolitical upheaval. For now, the differences are more pronounced in diagnosis than in policy prescriptions. All favor deepening alliances and partnerships, modernizing the military, fixing the defense industrial base, strengthening deterrence, tackling transnational challenges such as global public health, and pursuing hardheaded diplomacy with rivals.

Centrists also agree that Trump has severely weakened U.S. power and institutions, although they remain relatively optimistic about the country’s capacity to recover. But most recognize that the world the next Democratic president would inherit in 2029 is not the world that Biden inherited in 2021. Winning an election will not mean the end of Trumpism. The “America first” movement will likely remain a dominant force in the Republican Party, and the United States’ allies and partners will have to hedge against dramatic shifts in U.S. foreign policy from one election to the next. Even if a Democratic president can rebuild American power and repair damaged institutions, restoring international confidence in the durability of U.S. commitments will be much harder.

Winning an election will not mean the end of Trumpism.

The party’s progressives argue that the U.S. foreign policy establishment failed over the past 25 years by pursuing U.S. primacy at all costs. They see the U.S.-led order as deeply flawed in its design and track record, arguing that Washington’s selective application of the “rules-based order” undermined the order itself. As Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, of New York, put it at the Munich Security Conference in 2026, “In a rules-based order, hypocrisy is vulnerability.” They favor a rules-based order that applies its principles consistently, even if doing so constrains the United States.

Many progressives, led by Bernie Sanders, the independent senator from Vermont, also believe that a global oligarchy poses a threat to democracy and see big business in defense, technology, and finance as part of a corrupt system. They believe that corporate interests have driven excessive military spending, misguided interventions, and a global economy that favors multinational companies over workers.

Progressives see the turmoil of the past two years as accelerating the emergence of a multipolar order, in which the United States has an important, but more limited, role to play. According to the progressive thinker Ben Rhodes, a former deputy national security adviser to President Barack Obama, Washington should “re-engage the world as something other than a hegemon.” Americans are accustomed to seeing the country as an overall force for good, even when it uses military power, but progressives point to U.S. support for Israel’s war in Gaza, and the Trump administration’s actions in Iran and Venezuela as evidence of the enormous damage that interventionism can cause. Many argue that the United States should go to war only in self-defense—and with congressional authorization, as the Constitution requires. They also favor cuts to what they see as a bloated defense budget that encourages presidents to default to military action instead of diplomacy.

New debates, both between and within the various camps of the Democratic Party, are emerging.

Most progressives believe that the greatest threats to American security and prosperity are increasingly transnational rather than geopolitical: runaway artificial intelligence, climate change, and widening inequality, as enumerated by Sanders earlier this year. They argue that the threat from China is often overblown and that deterrence can be achieved and U.S. interests protected with existing capabilities and without a ratcheting up of tensions. As such, most progressives would prioritize cooperation with other powers, especially Beijing, on existential challenges over competition.

A distinct group of thinkers, usually aligned with the progressive camp, identifies with the restraint school of foreign policy. They tend to agree with the centrists about the centrality of geopolitics but want to reduce the United States’ exposure to it. They argue that Washington’s pursuit of military primacy has overstretched the country, unnecessarily embroiling it in conflicts and crises, and favor a more selective approach that focuses on a smaller number of vital interests, reduces overseas commitments, and emphasizes diplomacy, even if it leads to outcomes abroad that conflict with their values.

Despite these differing worldviews, there is much agreement between centrists and progressives. Both camps support NATO, the EU, and Washington’s alliances in the Indo-Pacific. Both want to stand up to Russian President Vladimir Putin and help Ukraine. Both oppose the Iran war and both want to root out corruption. But new debates, both between and within the various camps of the Democratic Party, are steadily emerging alongside those that have historically divided the party.

SHOCK OF THE NEW

One of the most important debates currently unfolding in the party is the United States’ relationship with Israel and Washington’s role in the Middle East more generally. This is likely to be the most pronounced break from the Biden administration. Many Democrats blame Biden for not doing enough to restrain Israel in the Gaza war and some former senior Biden administration officials even acknowledge that they should have done more.

Many centrists identify Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as the driving force behind a series of Israeli actions that have hurt U.S. interests, such as advocating all-out war against Iran, using excessive force in Gaza, and undermining the Palestinian Authority, and they recommend adjusting U.S. policy accordingly. They believe that Netanyahu’s departure could create an opening for a broader regional settlement, but that Washington would still need to exert pressure on Israel to make progress toward Palestinian statehood. The potential presidential candidate Rahm Emanuel, for instance, has proposed a regional initiative in which the United States would support a Palestinian state in exchange for full Arab recognition of Israel and closer strategic and economic ties across the region. Such an initiative would include forceful U.S. opposition to effective Israeli annexation of the West Bank, backed by sanctions on violent settlers and the entities that build or finance illegal settlements. Emanuel would also end U.S. defense subsidies for Israel, making it purchase weapons on the same terms as other allies.

Other centrists go further. Jon Finer, the former principal deputy national security adviser to Biden, has argued for more sustained pressure on Israel regardless of whether Netanyahu is replaced. The United States must make Israel choose “between the abundant and irreplaceable benefits of the U.S. relationship and the indefensible policies that are driving a wedge between our societies,” Finer wrote recently in The New York Times. This would include treating the occupied territories as different from Israel proper, imposing sanctions on individuals and entities involved in settlement expansion, and conditioning arms sales on Israeli compliance with international humanitarian law.

Progressives have largely welcomed centrists’ changes on Israel.

Few elected Democrats still argue for unconditional support, but a group that emphasizes the value of the U.S.-Israeli alliance and favors lower levels of pressure on Israel will likely remain by 2028. For instance, these centrists would sanction violent settlers, as the Biden administration did, but may not target the banks that finance the construction of new settlements. They would give a new prime minister the benefit of the doubt, should one successfully form a coalition. But if Netanyahu remains in power during the U.S. primary campaign, their position would be hard to sustain.

Many centrists aim to reduce the U.S. military commitment to the Middle East, but they reject the idea of simply walking away from the region. As Philip Gordon, the former national security adviser to Vice President Harris, put it in Foreign Affairs, the United States should “defend a narrower set of core interests with a smaller military footprint, more diplomacy, more alternatives, and more partners.” Centrists are divided over how exactly to do this; some would be open to a defense treaty with Saudi Arabia if it were part of a broader move toward a Palestinian state, whereas others want to avoid new defense commitments. A small group of centrist dissenters, especially those who are primarily concerned about China, see the Middle East as quicksand that stymies U.S. interests in Asia and are more willing to countenance a significant reduction of forces.

Progressives have largely welcomed centrists’ changes on Israel, even if many are skeptical that they would actually follow through on their rhetoric once in power. They tend to see Finer’s support for more sustained pressure on Israel and increased engagement with Palestinians as a good starting point. But many go further. Intraprogressive arguments focus on whether to support Israel’s access to defensive weaponry, such as the Iron Dome missile defense system and whether a Palestinian state should be recognized on day one of a Democratic administration or should be the ultimate goal of a diplomatic initiative. Others favor more radical change. The progressive commentator Peter Beinart, for example, has argued that a two-state solution is no longer viable and progressives should support a single state with equal rights for Palestinians and Jewish Israelis. Some progressives question whether Israel is an ally at all and believe it has little to offer the United States.

AI safety could become one of the most consequential issues in the primary.

More generally, progressives increasingly favor a complete withdrawal of U.S. forces from the Middle East and distancing the United States from its Gulf allies. As Michael Fuchs, Harris’s former deputy chief of staff, wrote in Foreign Affairs, it is “long past time for the United States to withdraw its forces from the Middle East, stop arming governments that violate U.S. and international law, and end its role as guarantor of regional order.”

Israel may be the source of the most contentious division among Democrats, but it is not the only one. AI has also emerged as a source of disagreement, although the battle lines are not so neatly drawn. One group of influential centrists, which includes many Biden administration officials, sees AI as a technology whose benefits are as world-changing as its risks. They believe that the United States must win the race with China—often citing the cyber-capabilities of the Mythos model as an example—but also favor slowing down AI development to ensure that the models are safe and the economic effects, particularly on jobs, can be managed. To do this, they advocate strengthening U.S. export controls over China to provide the breathing room to “pace the frontier” and regulate leading labs. They want to negotiate a common position on AI with allies and partners (including by distributing AI infrastructure to the United States’ closest allies, such as Australia and Canada) and to open a dialogue with China to manage safety risks.

There were, however, significant disagreements within the Biden administration over how to compete technologically with China, which are likely to reemerge in the 2028 campaign. Biden’s Treasury Department questioned whether export controls could prevent China from catching up, arguing that maintaining Chinese dependence on American technology would preserve U.S. leverage and discourage Beijing from developing alternatives. Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo shared this skepticism, telling The Wall Street Journal in December 2024 that “trying to hold China back is a fool’s errand,” and that investing in industrial capacity in the United States mattered more than export controls. Other centrist Democrats, such as former National Security Adviser Susan Rice, have argued that the United States and China should negotiate an agreement to freeze AI models in place.

Progressives, meanwhile, are generally unpersuaded that the United States can win, or even needs to win, the frontier race against China. A minority are skeptical of the technology, dismissing the claims of frontier labs as hype, and believe that it can largely be managed with existing legal frameworks. Others, however, believe that the United States should halt AI development, impose a moratorium on new data centers, take an aggressive stance toward the technology companies, and negotiate a grand bargain with China resembling a comprehensive arms control agreement. Sanders and Representative Ro Khanna, of California, have both called for a binding agreement with Beijing to restrain the development of potentially dangerous AI systems, explicitly drawing parallels with Cold War nuclear arms control. Progressive members of Congress have mostly voted in favor of export controls on China, although it is unclear whether they would renew and strengthen them if China were to threaten retaliatory escalation early in a new administration.

AI safety could become one of the most consequential issues in the primary, creating new coalitions that cut across the traditional centrist-progressive divide. The pace of AI development and the likelihood of future AI-driven cyberattacks or loss-of-control incidents mean that the issue will remain particularly fluid in the lead-up to 2028.

OLD GRUDGES

Several long-standing debates between and within Democratic factions, including on some of the most important issues that the next Democratic president will face, remain unresolved, too. Chief among them is China.

Most centrists see China as the most significant strategic and economic challenge facing the United States, believing that it has a technological and manufacturing lead in many critical areas. They worry about a war over Taiwan but believe it can be avoided if the United States restores its national power, deepens its alliances, strengthens Taiwan’s self-defense and resilience, selectively pushes back against China when necessary, and injects some stability into the relationship through high-level diplomacy—an approach that the Biden administration called “managed competition.” They are actively debating how to expand Biden-era efforts, particularly with respect to alliances and export controls, and how much the United States should dial up its competitive efforts without undermining diplomacy and risking a spiral into confrontation. Although most centrists favor some variant of Biden’s managed competition strategy, some associated with the camp, such as Ryan Hass, who served on Obama’s National Security Council, have cautioned that “attempting to restore or make minor updates to the status quo that existed before Trump’s second term—or to go even further in an effort to project ostensible strength—would be misguided.”

Progressives see centrists’ strategic competition frame as excessively hawkish and as a self-fulfilling prophecy. They believe that Washington and Beijing have a shared interest in tackling shared challenges, particularly AI safety and climate change and that détente is an achievable goal. Some, including Jessica Chen Weiss, a professor at Johns Hopkins University’s School for Advanced International Studies who served on the State Department’s Policy Planning staff during the Biden administration, think that Washington should pursue that goal by deepening economic ties with China, ceasing discussion of the strategic competition, and nurturing moderates in the United States and China. Most progressives do not recommend accommodating China’s geopolitical ambitions, but they believe that Washington can reduce the risk of Chinese aggression by exercising restraint and engaging in high-level diplomacy. For progressives, deterrence can be more readily accomplished than centrists believe, both because the United States’ existing military power is sufficient and because China is not an aggressive revisionist power like Russia.

There are significant divisions among progressives over the economic threat from China.

The debate over China is closely linked to another debate over foreign economic policy and trade. Biden’s shift toward industrial policy and supply chain resilience was partly driven by a belief that China’s unfair trading practices merited a fundamental change in U.S. policy. Many centrists now argue for an expansion of industrial policy to cover a wider variety of critical goods, such as robotics. They want to make common cause with Europe to respond to Chinese overcapacity, including by coordinating tariffs and import bans on emerging technologies and by integrating their manufacturing efforts to compete with Beijing. Some, such as the former deputy national security adviser Daleep Singh, have advocated for a sovereign wealth fund to kick-start investment in new technologies. They are perturbed by Trump’s use of coercive economic power against allies and are developing their own doctrine of economic statecraft with appropriate safeguards. Some centrists want to grant allies and partners more access to the U.S. market, not through the expansive multilateral agreements that defined the 1990s and early 2000s but through smaller, more targeted agreements.

There are significant divisions among progressives over the economic threat from China. Elected officials on the left tend to see trade policy toward China very similarly to centrists. Lawmakers such as Khanna, Sanders, and Senator Elizabeth Warren, of Massachusetts, are also concerned about deindustrialization and China’s dominance of advanced manufacturing and favor stronger measures against Beijing’s unfair trade practices. But progressive foreign policy thinkers are often more skeptical of economic confrontation and favor closer ties with China. Some support industrial policy but are uneasy about framing it principally around competition with China. They recommend pursuing industrial policy for other reasons, such as tackling inequality or climate change, and believe that the United States and China can work together on global economic issues, including Sanders’s proposal for a global minimum wage.

Democrats are likely to disagree on what to do with Trump’s tariffs toward allies and partners, although few talk about it openly. Some say that the next president should describe Trump’s tariffs as an unfair tax on American consumers and lift them immediately and unilaterally. Others may favor keeping some of the tariffs to protect certain industries or as a revenue stream to fund their own domestic priorities. And a third group says that the next administration should lift them as part of a quick negotiation with allies on a common position on economic and technological issues relating to China, including dealing with the overcapacity problem and restoring export controls on China’s compute power.

Different perceptions of China also inform the party’s internecine debates on climate policy. Progressives see climate as one of the top priorities for a new administration, not subordinated to national security goals, and thus prioritize cooperating with China, including on electric vehicles and clean technology. Centrists, however, are skeptical that China will be a reliable climate partner, oppose Chinese electric vehicles on national security grounds, and favor cooperation with smaller groups of like-minded nations as a more dependable way to advance clean technologies.

This disagreement is just one dimension of a deeper split on how best to address climate change. Centrists tend to argue that Democrats should connect climate to affordability, jobs, and energy security rather than making it the organizing principle of the governance agenda. They favor investing in clean technology, although some are more open to natural gas and permitting changes that they say will speed construction. Progressives believe that supporting clean technology is necessary but insufficient and call for policies that reduce the supply of oil and gas.

WORK IT OUT

The centrist-progressive debate runs deeper than a disagreement over policy. It is a question of how the United States can achieve peace and prosperity: by managing geopolitical rivalries and the instabilities stemming from the unraveling of the international order or by overcoming geopolitics through cooperation.

If the party does not have these debates openly and consistently over the next two years, a Democratic president risks entering office in 2029 much as Jimmy Carter did in 1977. Carter inherited an international environment in which the Nixon-Kissinger framework of détente was under increasing strain. His administration was divided between the competing worldviews of National Security Adviser Zbigniew Brzezinski, who favored a more confrontational approach to the Soviet Union, and Secretary of State Cyrus Vance, who emphasized diplomacy and arms control. Heated disagreements between the camps repeatedly complicated Carter’s efforts to develop and implement a coherent strategy toward Moscow.

A repeat of the situation in 2029 could be even more damaging. The next president will inherit frayed alliances, mounting Chinese pressure on Taiwan, deepening integration and cooperation among Washington’s adversaries, and potential wars in Iran and Ukraine, not to mention new crises that may emerge over the next two years. Failure to settle on a clear agenda could paralyze U.S. decision-making at precisely the time when a new administration will want to provide strong leadership and direction.

Fortunately, centrists and progressives have considerable common ground. They both are committed to rebuilding the foundations of American power, supporting alliances, backing a just peace in Ukraine, taking transnational challenges seriously, and eschewing unnecessary military interventions. They may not reach a partywide consensus on every issue. But a spirited, productive primary debate will allow voters to make an informed choice and ensure that the first year of the next administration is spent acting on a vision, not arguing over one.

title: Dialogue, Trust, and Learning in the Age of AI: Why Students Belong at the Table
summary:
On a Tuesday morning last semester, students in my Writing II class engaged in debate. After the topic of AI and college classes came up, a spokesperson for one group, a young woman, spoke up from the back of the room, beginning with “I’m in college for a reason.” She said, “Sure, I could ask […]

The post Dialogue, Trust, and Learning in the Age of AI: Why Students Belong at the Table appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
On a Tuesday morning last semester, students in my Writing II class engaged in debate. After the topic of AI and college classes came up, a spokesperson for one group, a young woman, spoke up from the back of the room, beginning with “I’m in college for a reason.” She said, “Sure, I could ask ChatGPT to summarize an article for me, but how does that build my analytical skills?”

She continued; we listened (and I found myself internally nodding yes to each point she made). In those moments, I felt myself relax, the opposite of the usual apprehension I feel when AI is being touted by PD-pitchers or debated among teachers. I thought – This is what has been missing: the student voice.

Our AI-infused world has ushered in a sense of vertigo; that is, technology has moved faster than our understanding of its implications. To pretend any educator or institution has the singular, right approach to the ever-evolving AI availability is disingenuous. The approach does not exist, and we have been figuring out that our early efforts to combat students’ unethical AI use are falling short. The surveillance tactics and fear-messaging have not curbed AI use. We know checkers can be faulty, and trust between teachers and students has been negatively impacted (Luo).

It is easy to understand how the varied responses to AI across institutions, society, and classrooms have left students feeling confused, causing many to stay silent while attempting to discern how much AI use, if any, crosses the line.

For example, this past May, commencement speakers at multiple graduation ceremonies were booed for their references to AI. This includes a business executive who was booed by arts and humanities graduates after referring to the rise of AI as “the next industrial revolution” (Shahin).

All students deserve a voice in discussions about AI, including those who question its larger implications and those who embrace its potential as a learning tool. Students are navigating the same often conflicting landscape as teachers and higher ed administrators. With more student participation in these conversations, perhaps we can turn the page from reactive responses to proactive engagement.

My own students, along with those whose voices we hear at commencements and across digital platforms, offer a collective reminder: few groups have as much at stake in the future of AI as Generation Z, and from their front row seat, they see that in higher education, approaches to AI run the gamut – from signed “I will not use AI” contracts and blue-book essays to “cite your use of AI.”

Teachers also observe the wide range of responses in higher education. The last few years, most conversations with my English colleagues have involved our efforts to try to AI-proof our online writing classes – with emphasis on the word try. As AI becomes more pervasive, we are all grappling with the same core questions: How do we protect human creativity, judgment, and connection? How do continue to make learning meaningful? As my student reminded me, students are in college for a reason.

For me, as I have (more or less) left behind the use of AI checkers, I’m ready for less AI surveillance. I prefer to use that energy for increased dialogue with my students about what learning requires. I am ready for more two-sided conversations, student reflection, and shared inquiry into what represents true learning. And I will continue to encourage students to own their own writing and to emphasize how – in their written compositions – their voice makes the difference.

Trust Between Students and Teachers

Over the last few years, I have attended multiple professional development meetings tied to AI literacy. Few included students’ comments. My own student’s observation (“I’m in college for a reason”) made me consider my own voice and how relaxed I have become with waiting for direction from higher ups.

Math teacher Al Rabanera writes about a similar wake-up call: “I didn’t realize how much agency I had lost as a California teacher until AI showed me what I’d been missing.” Rabanera said AI revealed “how comfortable [he had] become with waiting. Waiting for district guidance. . . . Waiting to be told not just what to do, but how to think.”

As this past academic year concluded, one other reflection lingered with me: A heavy emphasis on warnings about AI use, followed by detection and required meetings with students who submitted AI-written drafts, particularly in my online non-synchronous classes, tainted the spirit of the classes. As Matthew Brophy points out, “When pedagogy tilts toward detection over development, it cultivates a classroom ethos of suspicion rather than community.”

Jess Luo explains, ”Trusting relationships between teachers and students are crucial in developing effective teaching, learning and assessment,” and “there is discernible concern among the higher education community that GenAI is causing an ‘erosion of trust’ between students and their teachers.”

Below are strategies to reset the table and to turn the focus of classes in the age of AI from “accusatory ambience [that] breeds anxiety” (Brophy) to purposeful, fun engagement.

Beginning-of-the-Semester Reflection

Ask students to reflect on their educational and career goals; to reflect on what they will learn in the course and the skills they will obtain. What challenges do they anticipate? What are strategies to offset those obstacles? In sum, their reflection of goals should reinforce for them why it is meaningful to be in college.

This early reflection aligns with what Pauline Stamp refers to as “Purpose-First Learning.” She suggests that teachers start day one by inviting students “to engage each learning objective [of the course]” and answer questions like “What does this objective mean to you? Why does it matter—personally, professionally, or socially?” Stamp points out that “engagement . . . emerges when learners understand why the learning matters to them.”

Ask students to reflect on their AI use – both in their private lives and in academia. Use reflection survey results to generate discussion about AI – the ways it is used in our personal lives, the mixed messaging that surrounds it, and the ethical/non-ethical use of it in college classes. This discussion needs to be a dialogue.

Student reflections, individual and collective, open the door for more conversations. When students are engaged, when they can see the value of the work, they are more likely to sit with an assignment, to analyze a prompt closely, and to seize ownership of their writing. Conversely, a Swansea University study concludes that “disengaged students are more likely to use AI tools—particularly ChatGPT—for academic assignments.”

Other strategies to build trust and investment in a class are not new and long predate the heavy AI influx:

Along with increased dialogue, provide students with clear guidance on each assignment.

Return students’ work quickly.

Facilitate opportunities for students to reflect on their own growth in the course.

When possible, comment on work in stages.

Provide individualized feedback to students; look for opportunities to point them toward paper topics and/or experiential learning opportunities that are likely to be of interest.

From my vantage point, as some of the smoke begins to clear in the AI-infused era, what has been missing are student voices. Students are living with the realities of AI every day. They deserve a genuine seat at the table in discussions about learning and technology. Meaningful learning depends on classrooms built on trust, dialogue, and shared reflection rather than fear or suspicion. The adage still rings true: We learn as much from our students as they do from us. My student this past spring inspired me not only to remember that students are in college for a reason but also to recall my own agency as a teacher and to encourage students to harness their own voices.

Dr. Mary Ruth Wallen brings over three decades of college teaching experience to her work. A native of Inez, Kentucky, she holds dual B.A. degrees in English and Journalism from Morehead State University (1995), an M.A. in English with a creative writing emphasis from Indiana State University (1997), an MFA in Fiction from Southern Illinois University–Carbondale (2003), and a Doctorate of Arts in English Pedagogy from Murray State University (2021). Since 2003, she has been teaching at Big Sandy Community and Technical College in Prestonsburg, KY. Dr. Wallen believes that strong writing transcends genre and empowers all who practice it.

Daniels, Anton. “Woman says Gen Z are idiots, don’t know how to do anything without AI helping them in the classroom ….” Facebook, 15 May 2026, https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=4390448791283373. Accessed 26 May 2026.
