title: ‘Being to Learn’ Rather Than ‘Learning to Be’: Shifting Thinking About Authentic Assessment
summary:
Emerging from tensions created by theory–practice gap rhetoric, authentic assessment has been heralded as a pedagogical vaccine. The post ‘Being to Learn’ Rather Than ‘Learning to Be’: Shifting Thinking About Authentic Assessment appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
Emerging from tensions created by theory–practice gap rhetoric, authentic assessment has been heralded as a pedagogical vaccine. Now firmly embedded in the vernacular of higher education, authentic assessment offers learning designers a rich pool of innovative possibilities. These approaches have been shown to boost student engagement while offering academics a defense of the relevance of their assessment designs. At its core, authentic assessment involves designing tasks that mirror real-world challenges, helping students develop the knowledge and skills they’ll need beyond graduation. We usually find such tasks embedded within existing curricula and programs, as common fixtures of what we describe here as the ‘learning to be’ paradigm; the process of helping students acquire the knowledge and skills of a profession.

However, regardless of how novel an authentic assessment may be, while it remains a feature of traditional university systems thinking, it may contribute to the same divide it seeks to bridge. Central to this dilemma is the argument that the issue lies not in the quality of innovation, but in the divergent objectives and priorities of the modern campus and the workplace. Put simply, it is not the tool but the context in which it is used. While ‘learning to be’ approaches emphasise knowledge and skills acquisition, they often overlook the attributes and qualities most valued by employers.

To illustrate this disconnect, consider the following industry priorities.

Discrete Sample of Knowledge or Skills

Authentic assessment captures insights into students’ optimized efforts at a single time point, typically reflecting content knowledge or specific skills. In contrast, workplaces value consistency, reliability, and personal attributes, where a worker’s weakest area may shape perceptions of their competence.

Attendance and Punctuality

Academic staff increasingly contend with low student attendance, with flexible learning measures accommodating participation on students’ terms. In contrast, the professional world is far less forgiving, where punctuality and reliability are non-negotiable.

Work Deadlines

Many academics now anticipate a surge of extension requests as due dates approach. Institutional policies often allow automated approvals to support student success. Conversely, workplaces depend on work being delivered on time and within budget, with employees held accountable.

Direction vs. Initiative

Employers value initiative and self-directed action. Yet, when authentic assessments remain highly prescriptive, students may become passive, awaiting instruction rather than demonstrating independence.

Engaging with Critical Feedback and Grade Appeals

Employers expect individuals to respect expertise and respond constructively to feedback. In contrast, students may challenge or negotiate grades, exposing authentic assessments to cultural inconsistencies.

Narrow Scope and Censored Feedback

Assessment workloads and the need for defensible grading often lead to standardized responses. While transparent, these may restrict nuanced feedback and shield students from the candid critiques encountered in professional practice.

Student Comfort Zones

Students often control where they sit, who they work with, and how tasks are completed. In professional settings, individuals must adapt to unfamiliar colleagues and environments.

It is argued that solutions to these disparities reside in the coexistence of higher education and industry cultures, supported by an elevated awareness of expectations. This requires subtle shifts within authentic assessment philosophy.

The “Being to Learn” Philosophy

One solution lies in a fundamental shift in pedagogical thinking—moving beyond what students need to learn or do to consider who they need to become and how they must act. This is not a call to withdraw essential supports, but an invitation to infuse professional expectations throughout the student journey. If universities are to bridge education and employment, they must illuminate the often-unspoken norms of professional life and provide opportunities for students to develop them.

The “Being to Learn” approach recognises that professional identity formation requires immersive, sustained support beyond a single embedded task. It reflects an intentional effort to design experiences that engage students in the how of working, not just the what.

Below are suggestions that embody this philosophy:

Clearly Describe Future Work

Frame assessments beyond content, incorporating professional contexts such as shift work, remote practice, client expectations, and role demands.

Refer to the Rule Book

Use standards from professional bodies and regulators to anchor authentic assessment design.

Real Assessment Demands Real Feedback

Provide candid, meaningful feedback aligned with workplace expectations.

Highlight Attendance and Punctuality

Encourage reflection on the professional consequences of lateness or absence.

Encourage Experimentation

Design tasks that require initiative, innovation, and independent problem-solving.

Speak the Language

Introduce disciplinary terminology to support professional identity formation.

Promote a Classroom Code of Conduct

Encourage professional behaviours, collaboration, and respectful engagement.

Embrace Discomfort

Rotate groups and require students to work with unfamiliar peers to build adaptability.

Authentic assessment has enhanced the relevance of higher education assessment practices, but it is not a silver bullet. To truly prepare students for life beyond university, we must shift from preparing them to complete tasks to helping them become professionals. The “Being to Learn” philosophy offers a powerful next step by bridging learning, identity, and action in pursuit of meaningful and enduring educational outcomes.

Dr. James Thompson is a senior lecturer in the School of Pharmacy and Biomedical Science at Adelaide University in South Australia. For several decades he has been a champion for advancing the assessment practices and decision making about the competency and the work-readiness of graduates across health disciplines. He has contributed original theory and insights which have been broadly adopted in the practice of others.

title: When Student Laptops Fall Behind, Campus IT Can Close the Gap
summary:

In a recent NVIDIA survey of 1,000 U.S. undergraduates, 61% of respondents said their coursework has become more demanding, and 64% are running multiple demanding applications daily. Additionally, 77% of students said their major shaped their laptop choice. These numbers will continue to climb as artificial intelligence–assisted work and AI-focused areas of study become standard. “This disconnect shows up as soon as coursework goes beyond web apps,” says Carney-Morris, the college’s director of educational technology and chair of the Association for Computing Machinery’s Special Interest Group on University and College Computing Services.

Budget devices can also struggle with statistical analysis, modeling, media production and geographic information systems. Before recommending a replacement, she suggests running the same assignment on a lab computer over wired Ethernet, then campus Wi-Fi, to isolate the problem.

“This helps identify if the bottleneck is the assignment, the network or the student’s device,” she says.

From there, IT teams can address the specific barrier while keeping students connected to coursework.

Forecast Needs With Faculty

Carney-Morris says she recommends aligning academic planning with institutional budget and equipment refresh cycles. At Lewis & Clark, summer lab refreshes make the end of spring term an important checkpoint with faculty, lab managers, security teams and service desk staff.

Relationships with early adopters give IT advance notice of assignments and AI tools that might expose limitations in student-owned devices.

Ed Skoudis, president of the SANS Technology Institute, says he recommends testing faculty-created exercises on the hardware students use. Instructors working on powerful computers may not encounter the delays their students experience.

“When we design labs, we try to support systems as much as 3 or 4 years old,” he says.

Requirements also vary within disciplines. Digital forensics exercises may need substantial storage for memory and file system images, while penetration testing can demand more central processing unit and graphics processing unit (GPU) capacity.

Testing can reveal opportunities to reduce a data set or adjust software settings while preserving the learning objective. IT and faculty can explore those changes before raising device requirements.

Recommend What Students Actually Need

Jennifer Mathes, CEO of the Online Learning Consortium, recommends mapping computing requirements across programs and identifying when students will encounter more demanding applications.

“Recommendations should be reviewed regularly by IT and academic departments, but they should not automatically become more demanding simply because new technology is available,” she says.

Guidance should distinguish minimum specifications, recommended configurations and specialized program requirements. It should also explain when capabilities become necessary and whether shared resources offer an alternative.

In addition, AI coursework does not automatically require a new laptop, because browser-based AI services have different hardware demands from local model development or advanced data analysis, Mathes notes.

She recommends institutions assess whether investment in shared infrastructure would serve students better than requiring individual upgrades.

Match Resources to Coursework

Mathes says loaners can address temporary failures or short-term financial barriers, while shared labs support expensive specialized applications. Virtual desktops provide access to more powerful computing but depend on connectivity and licensing.

One-to-one programs can provide consistent access across a program, provided institutions establish sustainable funding. Budgets must include support, maintenance, replacement cycles and accessibility.

“Virtual desktop infrastructure with GPU support allows students to access specialized applications without needing a high-end machine or a trip to a specialized lab,” he explains.

Coordinating those services requires departments to agree on what coursework demands and how students will obtain access.

“The budget conversation works best when IT, student services and department managers are aligned, treating device access as a shared institutional priority, not a siloed IT expense,” Rocco says.

Support Access, Measure Results

Nicole Muscanell, senior researcher at EDUCAUSE, cautions that providing equipment alone cannot resolve every access problem.

“In our research, the most common issue overall is access to internet and Wi-Fi, with students calling for increased reliability, speed and coverage across campus,” she says.

Help desks should clearly identify supported devices, applications and services, alongside routes for resolving problems beyond their scope. Expanded hours, self-service resources and after-hours triage can help students obtain assistance when assignments are due.

title: The under-16 audience you still need to reach
summary: Your future applicants may start thinking about university years before they apply. Reaching under-16s means taking a different approach, with useful content and privacy-conscious digital journeys that help younger students explore what higher education could look like for them.
full_text:
Your next applicant may be 14 today.

They might already be thinking about subjects they enjoy, careers they could see themselves doing and whether university feels like somewhere they belong. By the time they arrive on your undergraduate course pages, quite a few of those ideas will already have taken shape.

So how do you reach students earlier without treating a 14-year-old like a recruitment lead?

Start earlier, but differently

Higher education outreach has been doing this for years. School visits, subject tasters, summer schools and campus experiences give younger students a chance to see what university is actually like, often well before they need to make an application decision.

The University of Southampton, for example, runs a dedicated pre-16 outreach programme, including Year 10 subject tasters and a residential where students can stay in halls, explore different subjects and experience campus life. citeturn435439search0turn435439search9

At this age, you're helping students answer much earlier questions. What could I study? Where might this subject take me? Could someone like me go to university?

"Under 16" isn't really one audience. What interests a 12-year-old student will be quite different from what a 15-year-old wants to know.

Your content should reflect that.

The University of Derby takes a longer view with its Progress to Success programme, working with students from Years 7 to 11. Younger pupils get an introduction to university through experience days, while later activities include subject sessions, mentoring and a Year 10 residential. "

Reach the people around them

For younger students, your audience is bigger than the student themselves.

Parents and carers may be trying to understand subject choices, university costs or what opportunities are available.

Teachers and careers advisers need resources they can use in school. Community groups can introduce higher education to young people who may not encounter it through the usual recruitment channels.

That gives your university or college plenty of ways to be useful without needing to communicate directly with every young person.

You could create a simple parent guide, give teachers ready-made classroom activities, run an online session through a school or invite a youth group onto campus.

And make the content easy to share. A useful guide shouldn't have to sit behind a form. If a teacher wants to print it, a parent wants to send it to someone else or a careers adviser wants to add it to a school portal, let them.

Give them something to experience

There's only so much a webpage can tell a 14-year-old about university.

A day on campus can do a lot more.

Subject tasters, lab sessions, creative workshops and opportunities to meet current students can turn a fairly abstract idea of “university" into something much easier to picture.

You don't need to recreate an open day for Year 9 or Year 10. Give students the chance to try something interesting, see spaces they wouldn't normally see and ask the questions they actually have.

Online experiences can work well too. Webinars such as What is university really like?, How do school subjects connect to degrees? or Careers you may not have heard of can be shared through schools and parents without expecting a young person to follow your social accounts first.

Lancaster University also starts well before application age, with outreach for Years 7–10. That includes student role models at careers events, workshops helping Year 9 students think about subjects and higher education, and campus visits for Year 10. You can give younger students the information that makes sense to them now, then build on it later.

Take another look at your forms

This is also a good time to look at what happens when a younger visitor reaches your website.

Imagine a 14-year-old has found your engineering content and wants to know more. Do they really need to give you their phone number, home address, intended entry year and several other pieces of personal information?

Probably not.

Most exploratory content can be open. Where registration genuinely is needed — perhaps for a campus event — collect what you need to run it safely and involve the parent, guardian or school where appropriate.

The wider digital environment is moving firmly in this direction. The UK ICO's Children's Code says profiling should be switched off by default for children unless there is a compelling reason, while the EU's Digital Services Act prohibits targeted advertising to minors based on profiling.

For your digital team, that makes a privacy-conscious approach useful well beyond compliance. It encourages you to ask whether every field, cookie, automated journey and audience segment is actually helping the young person in front of you.

Think beyond the application

The awkward thing about under-16 outreach is that its value won't necessarily show up neatly in next year's applicant numbers.

And that's fine.

Look instead at which schools come back, whether families are using your resources, which activities students attend and whether your outreach is reaching the communities you hoped it would.

A young person who leaves one of your sessions understanding university a little better — even if they eventually study somewhere else — hasn't been a failed conversion.

They've had a useful interaction with your institution at a point when it could genuinely help.

Your future applicants are already out there, forming opinions about education long before application season begins.

title: When will the underrepresentation of Black professors end?
summary: by Zarus Cenac On the SRHE Blog, in May and July, I wrote about the underrepresentation of Black people amongst professors in the UK higher education sector. In response to my May blog post, a commentator brought up the idea … Continue reading →
full_text:
by Zarus Cenac

On the SRHE Blog, in May and July, I wrote about the underrepresentation of Black people amongst professors in the UK higher education sector. In response to my May blog post, a commentator brought up the idea of a time delay between “the demographics of academia” and “changes in the wider population”, and that “estimating what is a reasonable lag is challenging and probably highly contestable” (Golding, 2026, para. 1). The present blog post takes a step along that path. There is an underrepresentation of Black female professors and Black male professors (Paper Whispers, 2025; Figure 1) – for females and males separately, I estimate how many years it may take for the underrepresentation of Black professors to end (Figure 2). This is done by estimating when the percentage of professors who are Black will eventually match Black representation in part of the UK population who are around a certain age (Figure 2). I also look for an indication of whether underrepresentation has been tangibly improving for Black female professors and Black male professors (Figure 2). Additionally, I consider which is the better of two similar methods for calculating the percentage of professors who are Black (eg, Figure 4a and 4b).

Figure 1

The Underrepresentation of Black Female Professors and Black Male Professors in UK Higher Education Institutions

Note. Data (2024–25 academic year) from Higher Education Statistics Agency (HESA, nd-a) and 2021/2022 UK Census data (Office for National Statistics, 2025) were used regarding Figure 1 and in analysis. As before, statistical analysis was used to explore the representation of Black professors – see Box 1 for a description of this analysis.

Black representation over time: Professors

There have been observations on what the representation of Black professors looks like at different points in time (eg, Gibney, 2024; Rollock, 2025). For instance, between the 2021–22 and 2022–23 academic years, there was a 0.2% increase in the percentage of professors who are Black, with the percentage being 0.9% in 2022–23 (Gibney, 2024), and the percentage of female professors who are Black was 0.6% in 2019–20 and 0.8% in 2022–23 (Rollock, 2025).

I used HESA data for the academic years 2014–15 to 2024–25 (HESA, nd-a) to calculate the percentage of professors who are Black amongst females and amongst males (the green circles in Figure 2). Based on representation across those academic years, predictions were made for Black representation in academic years after 2024–25 by fitting a (quadratic) trendline to the data for females and for males – the trendline is the green, dotted line in Figure 2. Despite trendlines predicting a continued increase in Black representation in the professoriate, it should be expected that the percentage will plateau at some point (see the plateauing indicated in Figure 3 regarding non-professors).

Figure 2

Predicting When Black Professors are no Longer Underrepresented

Note. Underrepresentation is predicted to end in the academic year when dotted lines cross. HESA (nd-a) data and 2021/2022 UK Census data (Office for National Statistics, 2025) were used for Figures 2 and 4. HESA (nd-a) state the number of professors by ethnicity categories: Asian, Black, Mixed, Other, White, and unknown ethnicity. In Figure 2 (and Figure 1), the representation of Black professors was calculated only using persons of known ethnicity. Additionally, using Census data (Nomis, 2013; Office for National Statistics, 2025), for females and males, Black representation amongst 45-to-64-year-olds in the UK was i) estimated for 2011 and ii) calculated for 2021/2022 (Box 2). For simplicity, census year (Office for National Statistics, 2025) was treated as the year when the academic year starts, eg, with the 2021/2022 Census data treated as the 2021–22 academic year.

Black representation over time: 54.5-year-olds in the UK population

The representation of Black people is lower in the professoriate than amongst people in the UK population who are between 45 and 64 years old – an age range which should reflect the ethnic composition of the professoriate well enough (Cenac, 2026). The midpoint of this age range is 54.5 years of age. For females and males, UK Census data are available for various ages and age ranges, for example, 15 years old, 50-to-54 years old, and 65-to-69 years old (Office for National Statistics, 2025). I estimated the year when ages and age ranges are 54.5 years old. To estimate when an age range is 54.5 years old, I calculated the midpoint of the age range, for example, the midpoint for the 50-to-54 age range is 52 years – the midpoint was used to represent the entire age range.

For ages and age ranges, UK Census data (Office for National Statistics, 2025) were used to calculate the percentage of females and males in the UK population who are Black. Figure 2 shows those percentages and the year in which the age/midpoint is 54.5 years old (orange circles). To estimate/predict what Black representation is like amongst 54.5-year-olds in the UK population for females and males at various times, a moving average line was used – the line can be seen in Figure 2 as a line which is orange and dotted.

The estimated representation of Black people amongst 54.5-year-olds seems to be acceptable as a stand-in for Black representation in 45-to-64-year-olds in the UK in the recent past if we consider representation in 45-to-64-year-olds in 2021/2022 and estimated representation in 45-to-64-year-olds in 2011 (see Box 2).

Figure 3

Level of Black Representation in Non-Professors

Note. Data (which are of academics who are not professors) are from HESA (nd-a), and percentage representation was calculated from non-professors whose ethnicity is known.

Predicting an end to underrepresentation

The ethnic diversity of the UK has been predicted to be higher in 2051 than it was in 2001 (Rees et al, 2011). So, it should not be surprising that Black representation amongst 45-to-64-year-olds seems to have been increasing (see the purple circles in Figure 2). Therefore, when examining whether the underrepresentation of Black professors is improving, it is important to take into consideration changes in representation within the UK population (Figure 2). For females and males, between the academic years 2014–15 and 2024–25, the increase in the representation of Black professors does not seem to outpace the estimated increase in the representation of Black people who are around 54.5-years-old (Figure 2). Therefore, between those academic years, there appears to have been no tangible improvement in the underrepresentation of Black female professors and Black male professors.

It is possible to estimate the academic year when there will no longer be an underrepresentation. This can be done by seeing the academic year when dotted lines for professors and 54.5-year-olds cross over each other. That academic year is approximately 2043–44 for Black female professors and approximately 2037–38 for Black male professors. So, in the 2026–27 academic year, we are an estimated 17 years away from underrepresentation disappearing for Black female professors, and an estimated 11 years away for Black male professors.

Gains in Black representation amongst female and male academics who are not professors (Figure 3) suggest that there is reason to be optimistic that Black representation in the professoriate will increase for females and males. However, if Black representation amongst female non-professors is plateauing (at around 3.6%), then the trend amongst female non-professors (Figure 3a) does not bode well for an end to the underrepresentation of Black female professors by the early-to-mid 2040s (Figure 2a).

The percentage of professors who are Black, and the prediction of when underrepresentation disappears, depends on which of two (slightly different) methods is used to calculate the percentage (Figures 2 and 4). Using HESA data, the percentage of professors who are Black is calculated by dividing the number of Black professors by some sort of total number (eg, Gibney, 2024), and the two methods differ in how this total is defined (Figures 2 and 4).

Method 1: Known ethnicity only. When calculating the percentage representation of an ethnic group, or ethnic groups, the percentage can be calculated just from individuals for whom ethnicity is known (eg, HESA, 2026a). So, in this method, people of unknown ethnicity are not included in the total when calculating the percentage of professors who are Black (eg, Gibney, 2022; Figure 2).

Method 2: Overall. From looking at HESA (nd-a, 2026a) data, there seem to have been times when the percentage of professors who are Black (eg, Essilfie-Quaye et al, 2025; Gibney, 2024), or the percentage of female professors who are Black (Rollock, 2025), was calculated from a total number which includes people whose ethnicity is unknown. Under that method, when a percentage is calculated, a Black person could be part of the Black category or part of the unknown ethnicity category.

Compared to Method 1, Method 2 leads to a slightly lower percentage of professors who are Black (Figure 4a and 4b; also see Le Roux, 2022), and predicts that underrepresentation disappears a little further into the future (Figures 2 and 4). As briefly covered in my second blog post, the percentage of professors who are Black may seem smaller (but not very much smaller) than it really is. Method 2 would lead to a slightly further underestimation than Method 1 (Figure 4a and 4b). So, Method 1 may be a somewhat better method than Method 2 for considering the percentage representation of Black professors (eg, see Le Roux, 2022) and for estimating when underrepresentation will end.

Figure 4

Different Methods of Calculating the Percentage of professors who are Black

Note. For Figure 4c and 4d, analysis regarding Figure 2 was undertaken again, but without limiting analysis to professors of known ethnicity – it is predicted that Black professors will no longer be underrepresented by 2045–46 for females and 2038–39 for males. Considering data and literature (HESA, nd-a; Rollock, 2025), some of the percentages for Black female professors (overall) in Figure 4a are in Rollock (2025) to one decimal place.

Context and future research

There seems to be a dearth of literature which examines how percentage representation changes with time in academia and in the national population to see whether the extent of ethnic/racial underrepresentation in academia changes. So, it is hoped that the approach used in the present blog (Figure 2) is useful for exploring the underrepresentation of ethnic/racial groups in academia outside of Black professors. In previous research, a graph has shown 1) the number of geoscience PhDs gained by people in specific (underrepresented) ethnic/racial groups for various years (amongst the USA’s citizens or people with permanent residency in the country) and 2) the number of people in ethnic/racial groups in the USA for various years (Bernard & Cooperdock, 2018). The graph has been referred to when stating that, when considering four decades, “the representation of students from underrepresented minorities … has essentially been stagnant when compared with the proportion of the relevant groups in the US population” (Bernard & Cooperdock, 2018, pp. 292–293); the present blog post examines the percentage representation of Black people in the professoriate and in the UK population (Figure 2) – if not done so already, it may be useful to examine (across the years) the percentage representation of ethnic/racial groups in academia beyond the Black professoriate (eg, in achieving PhDs) alongside percentage representation at the national population level for an indication of whether ethnic/racial underrepresentation is changing and when the underrepresentation may stop.

In my first blog post, I described how a statistic known as Cohen’s h can quantify the extent that Black professors are underrepresented, and I considered how that statistic can be used to define when underrepresentation is no longer large enough to be noteworthy. Therefore, Cohen’s h could be used to estimate the academic year when the difference between Figure 2’s orange and green lines is no longer noteworthy – that year would likely be sooner than the year when underrepresentation is forecasted to stop.

Whilst this blog post predicts when underrepresentation will end for Black female professors and Black male professors (Figure 2), these predictions are not intended to be conclusive. Ideally, future census data (Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency, 2026; Office for National Statistics, 2026; Scotland’s Census, 2025) and HESA data (HESA, 2026b) will be used to update these predictions in the approaching years. Moreover, previous research on predicting the future representation of ethnic groups in the UK (Rees et al, 2011) suggests that the method for predicting an end to underrepresentation (Figure 2) can be refined.

Conclusion

There has been an increase in the percentage of the professoriate who are Black (Gibney, 2024). Nevertheless, there does not appear to have been a reduction in the underrepresentation of Black female professors or Black male professors between 2014–15 and 2024–25 (Figure 2). Despite this lack of reduction in underrepresentation, it is provisionally predicted that the underrepresentation of Black female professors and Black male professors will end in 2043–44 and 2037–38 respectively. However, the prediction for Black female professors seems unlikely given the plateauing indicated in the representation of Black female non-professors (Figure 3a). Hopefully, predictions will be strengthened through subsequent data and improved methodology; it is intended that this blog post encourages efforts to monitor and predict the underrepresentation of Black professors over time so that there can be a clear idea of where the situation is heading.

title: Google: Internetsuche gibt es für Schulen nur, wenn KI-Tools freigegeben sind
summary: Parallel zur Vorstellung neuer KI-Werkzeuge für Schulen hat Google klargestellt, dass Schulen, die sie sperren, auch die Internetsuche nicht nutzen können.
full_text:
close notice

This article is also available in English. It was translated with technical assistance and editorially reviewed before publication.

.

Google knüpft den Zugang von Schulen zur mit Abstand beliebtesten Suchmaschine der Welt an die eigenen KI-Funktionen: Wenn Schulleitungen ihren Schülerinnen und Schülern keine Freigabe für Googles KI-Technik ermöglichen, gibt es auch keinen Zugang zur Google-Suche. Das hat der US-Konzern gegenüber der New York Times erklärt, nachdem mit einem neuen Blogeintrag neue KI-Funktionen angekündigt wurden. Der Schritt trifft demnach den kompletten primären und sekundären Bildungsbereich, der den Kindergarten bis zur 12. Klasse umfasst und unter der Abkürzung „K-12“ zusammengefasst wird. Googles Bildungschef Chris Phillips begründete den Schritt gegenüber der US-Zeitung mit der engen Verzahnung von Suche und KI.

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Empfohlener redaktioneller Inhalt

Mit Ihrer Zustimmung wird hier ein externer Inhalt geladen.

Googles Ankündigung folgte jetzt auf eine Vorstellung der neuen Funktion „Guided Learning“, die die Internetsuche ergänzen soll. Damit sollen Schülerinnen und Schüler durch den Weg zu einer Lösung für ein bestimmtes Problem geführt werden, ohne dass ihnen die Lösung direkt angezeigt wird. Ein Pilotversuch in ausgewählten US-amerikanischen Schulen soll noch im November beginnen. Im Google Classroom soll die neue Funktion jetzt schon weltweit abrufbar sein. Lobende Worte zitiert der US-Konzern aus Kolumbien, Indien und Thailand. Der erklärt weiterhin, dass diese und andere KI-Funktionen für Schülerinnen und Schüler ab Anfang 2027 standardmäßig deaktiviert werden sollen. Schulleitungen müssten sie explizit aktivieren. Tun sie das nicht, gibt es aber eben keine Google-Suche. Laut NBC News können Schulen die Suche zwar einzeln und ohne weitere Gemini-Produkte freischalten. KI-Funktionen wie automatisch erzeugte Zusammenfassungen bleiben darin aber enthalten.

Aus New York gibt es nach dem Bericht der New York Times bereits deutliche Kritik an dem Vorgehen von Google. Der dortige Bürgermeister Zohran Mamdani hat auf Bluesky geschrieben: „Google versucht, seine Monopolstellung zu nutzen, um den Einsatz von KI an unseren öffentlichen Schulen durchzusetzen.“ Kein Unternehmen solle aber die Macht haben, „zu diktieren, wie wir unsere Kinder unterrichten“. Ähnlich äußerte sich die ehemalige Chefin der US-Handelsaufsicht FTC Lina Khan auf dem Kurznachrichtendienst X: „Während die Öffentlichkeit zunehmend Widerstand gegen den Einsatz von KI an Schulen leistet, macht Google deutlich, dass es diejenigen bestrafen wird, die sich nicht fügen“, schreibt sie dort.

title: Bye-bye Microsoft: Nextcloud und Ionos starten Bildungsplattform für Schulen
summary: Microsoft und Google sollen im Schulalltag künftig weniger selbstverständlich sein: Sechs Bundesländer setzen auf eine Open-Source-Plattform.
full_text:
Im Bemühen um mehr digitale Souveränität im Bildungswesen gehen sechs deutsche Bundesländer einen neuen Weg. Berlin, Bremen, Hamburg, Hessen, Nordrhein-Westfalen und Rheinland-Pfalz haben sich auf einen Rahmenvertrag für eine digital souveräne Open-Source-Bildungsplattform geeinigt, die ohne Software von US-Tech-Riesen wie Microsoft oder Google auskommt. Wie am Rande des Digital-Gipfels der Bundesregierung in Berlin bekannt wurde, bildet die Software des Stuttgarter Unternehmens Nextcloud die technische Basis. Der Hosting-Anbieter Ionos stellt die Infrastruktur bereit.

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Konkret sollen die Schulen und Schulbehörden dann mit der M365-Alternative Ionos Nextcloud Workspace arbeiten können, die Nextcloud und Ionos im vergangenen Jahr vorgestellt haben. Das umfasst eine breite Palette an Funktionen, darunter Dateiaustausch, Chat, Videokonferenzen, E-Mail, Kalender und Office-Anwendungen.

Die Beschaffung wird über die Genossenschaft govdigital eG abgewickelt, was es den Ländern ermöglicht, die Lösung ohne erneute Ausschreibungsverfahren zu beziehen. govdigital eG ist das zentrale Kooperationsbündnis öffentlicher IT-Dienstleister in Deutschland. Der Vertrag läuft zunächst über vier Jahre, wobei die Schulen und Schulbehörden der Länder laut Nextcloud-Mitteilung nicht zur Nutzung verpflichtet sind.

Abhängigkeit von Microsoft und Google reduzieren

Das Projekt markiert einen bedeutenden Schritt, um die Abhängigkeit von großen US-Konzernen zu verringern. Gerade im Schulalltag, in dem Schüler frühzeitig im Umgang mit digitalen Werkzeugen geprägt werden, sehen Experten die Gefahr langfristiger Bindungen an proprietäre Systeme. Die neue Plattform soll als datenschutzkonforme Alternative dienen, die insbesondere den Anforderungen der Datenschutz-Grundverordnung entspricht und Schutz vor dem Zugriff durch US-Behörden bietet, wie er etwa durch den US-CLOUD-Act ermöglicht wird.

Frank Karlitschek, Gründer und Geschäftsführer von Nextcloud, sieht in der Vereinbarung eine strategische Weichenstellung. Er betont, dass der öffentliche Sektor eine entscheidende Rolle bei der Etablierung europäischer Softwarelösungen spiele. „Wir brauchen europäische Champions, um digitale Souveränität zu erreichen und den europäischen Softwaresektor zu stärken“, sagte Karlitschek der dpa. Der Staat könne dabei als sogenannter Leuchtturm-Kunde fungieren, der durch seine Nachfrage den Aufbau solcher Alternativen erst ermögliche. „Wir benötigen auch keine Fördergelder, sondern einfach nur Leuchtturm-Kunden.“

title: Urteil in Cottbus: Lehrer schlägt Schüler – Bewährungsstrafe
summary: Der Musiklehrer war gegenüber einem Elfjährigen sowie zwei zwölf Jahre alten Jungen gewalttätig geworden. Dafür erhielt er ein Jahr und einen Monat Freiheitsstrafe auf Bewährung.
full_text:
Urteil in Cottbus :

Lehrer schlägt Schüler – Bewährungsstrafe

03.11.2026, 14:28Lesezeit: 1 Min.

Eine Statue der Justitia hält eine Waage in der Hand. (Symbolbild)dpa

Der Musiklehrer war gegenüber einem Elfjährigen sowie zwei zwölf Jahre alten Jungen gewalttätig geworden. Dafür erhielt er ein Jahr und einen Monat Freiheitsstrafe auf Bewährung.

Ein Lehrer ist wegen Körperverletzung von mehreren Schülern und wegen Bedrohung vom Amtsgericht Cottbus zu einer Bewährungsstrafe verurteilt worden. Der Mann, Quereinsteiger als Musiklehrer, sei im September 2023 in vier Fällen gewalttätig gegenüber Schülern an einer Cottbuser Oberschule geworden, urteilte das Gericht. Es verhängte ein Jahr und einen Monat Freiheitsstrafe auf Bewährung. Zudem muss der Angeklagte Schmerzensgeld zahlen: 100 Euro an einen Schüler, jeweils 200 Euro an zwei weitere.

Der Lehrer gab die Vorwürfe vor Gericht zu und entschuldigte sich. Er hatte den Angaben zufolge einen elfjährigen Jungen im Unterricht gegen die Hüfte getreten und mit der Hand gegen den Hinterkopf geschlagen. Der Junge musste im Krankenhaus behandelt werden. Zwei weitere Zwölfjährige bekamen von ihm Schläge. Zunächst war von zwei Opfern die Rede gewesen.

Die Jungen haben laut dem Verein Opferperspektive einen Migrationshintergrund. Ein mögliches rassistisches Motiv hatte die Polizei deswegen nach der Anzeige der Eltern bei den Ermittlungen geprüft. Im Prozess spielte der Vorwurf nur am Rande eine Rolle. Das Urteil ist noch nicht rechtskräftig.

Se quindi la dimensione media dell’impresa italiana fosse quella tedesca, stante la situazione attuale la nostra produttività media salirebbe del 17%, superando quella di Francia, Germania e dell’intera media Ue.

«La buona notizia è che le nostre imprese nelle dimensioni maggiori sono assolutamente eccellenti e che il problema del Paese è quello del mix tra big e microimprese. Ecco perché vogliamo sensibilizzare le aziende sul tema della crescita, una necessità per restare competitivi».
